{{Short description|Path on an edge-colored graph over which no color repeats}}
[[File:Wheel rainbow coloring.svg|thumb|300px|Rainbow coloring of a [[wheel graph]], with three colors. Every two non-adjacent vertices can be connected by a rainbow path, either directly through the center vertex (bottom left) or by detouring around one triangle to avoid a repeated edge color (bottom right).]]

In [[graph theory]], a [[Path (graph theory)|path]] in an [[Edge coloring|edge-colored graph]] is said to be '''rainbow''' if no color repeats on it. A graph is said to be '''rainbow-connected''' (or '''rainbow colored''') if there is a rainbow path between each pair of its [[Vertex (graph theory)|vertices]]. If there is a rainbow [[Path (graph theory)|shortest path]] between each pair of vertices, the graph is said to be '''strongly rainbow-connected''' (or '''strongly rainbow colored''').{{sfnp|Chartrand|Johns|McKeon|Zhang|2008}}

== Definitions and bounds ==

The '''rainbow connection number''' of a graph <math>G</math> is the minimum number of colors needed to rainbow-connect <math>G</math>, and is denoted by <math>\text{rc}(G)</math>. Similarly, the '''strong rainbow connection number''' of a graph <math>G</math> is the minimum number of colors needed to strongly rainbow-connect <math>G</math>, and is denoted by <math>\text{src}(G)</math>. Clearly, each strong rainbow coloring is also a rainbow coloring, while the converse is not true in general.

It is easy to observe that to rainbow-connect any connected graph <math>G</math>, we need at least <math>\text{diam}(G)</math> colors, where <math>\text{diam}(G)</math> is the [[Diameter (graph theory)|diameter]] of <math>G</math> (i.e. the length of the longest shortest path). On the other hand, we can never use more than <math>m</math> colors, where <math>m</math> denotes the number of [[Edge (graph theory)|edges]] in <math>G</math>. Finally, because each strongly rainbow-connected graph is rainbow-connected, we have that <math>\text{diam}(G) \leq \text{rc}(G) \leq \text{src}(G) \leq m</math>.

The following are the extremal cases:{{sfnp|Chartrand|Johns|McKeon|Zhang|2008}}
*<math>\text{rc}(G) = \text{src}(G) = 1</math> [[if and only if]] <math>G</math> is a [[complete graph]].
*<math>\text{rc}(G) = \text{src}(G) = m</math> if and only if <math>G</math> is a [[Tree (graph theory)|tree]].

The above shows that in terms of the number of vertices, the upper bound <math>\text{rc}(G) \leq n - 1</math> is the best possible in general. In fact, a rainbow coloring using <math>n - 1</math> colors can be constructed by coloring the edges of a [[spanning tree]] of <math>G</math> in distinct colors. The remaining uncolored edges are colored arbitrarily, without introducing new colors. When <math>G</math> is 2-connected, we have that <math>\text{rc}(G) \leq \lceil n/2 \rceil</math>.{{sfnp|Ekstein|Holub|Kaiser|Koch|2013}} Moreover, this is tight as witnessed by e.g. odd cycles. For every bridgeless graph <math>G</math> with radius <math>r</math>, <math>rc(G)\le r(r+2)</math>.<ref name=Basavaraju2014>{{cite journal | last1 = Basavaraju | first1 = M. | last2 = Chandran | first2 = L. S. | last3 = Rajendraprasad | first3 = D. | last4 = Ramaswamy | first4 = A. | title = Rainbow connection number and radius | journal = Graphs and Combinatorics | volume = 30 | issue = 2 | pages = 275-285 | date = 2014}}</ref>

The '''very strong rainbow connection number''' (<math>vsrc(G)</math>) is the minimum number of colors required to color the edges of a graph <math>G</math> such that every shortest path between any two vertices is a rainbow path. While approximating <math>vsrc(G)</math> for a general graph <math>G</math> is an NP-hard problem, it can be solved in polynomial time for certain graph classes, such as [[Cactus graph|cactus graphs]].<ref name=Chandran2025>{{cite journal| last1 = Chandran | first1 = L. S.| last2 = Das | first2 = A.| last3 = Issac | first3 = D.| title = Algorithms and Bounds for Very Strong Rainbow Coloring| journal = Bulletin of the Malaysian Mathematical Sciences Society| volume = 48| pages = 96| date = 2025| doi = 10.1007/s40840-025-01876-8| doi-access = free}}</ref>

== Exact rainbow or strong rainbow connection numbers ==
The rainbow or the strong rainbow connection number has been determined for some structured graph classes:
*<math>\text{rc}(C_n) = \text{src}(C_n) = \lceil n/2 \rceil</math>, for each [[integer]] <math>n \geq 4</math>, where <math>C_n</math> is the [[cycle graph]].{{sfnp|Chartrand|Johns|McKeon|Zhang|2008}}
*<math>\text{rc}(W_n) = 3</math>, for each integer <math>n \geq 7</math>, and <math>\text{src}(W_n) = \lceil n/3 \rceil</math>, for <math>n \geq 3</math>, where <math>W_n</math> is the [[wheel graph]].{{sfnp|Chartrand|Johns|McKeon|Zhang|2008}}

== Complexity ==
The problem of deciding whether <math>\text{rc}(G) = 2</math> for a given graph <math>G</math> is [[NP-complete]].{{sfnp|Chakraborty|Fischer|Matsliah|Yuster|2011}} Because <math>\text{rc}(G) = 2</math> if and only if <math>\text{src}(G) = 2</math>,{{sfnp|Chartrand|Johns|McKeon|Zhang|2008}} it follows that deciding if <math>\text{src}(G) = 2</math> is NP-complete for a given graph <math>G</math>.

== Variants and generalizations == 
Chartrand, Okamoto and Zhang{{sfnp|Chartrand|Okamoto|Zhang|2010}} generalized the rainbow connection number as follows. Let <math>G</math> be an edge-colored nontrivial connected graph of order <math>n</math>. A tree <math>T</math> is a ''rainbow tree'' if no two edges of <math>T</math> are assigned the same color. Let <math>k</math> be a fixed integer with <math>2 \leq k \leq n</math>. An edge coloring of <math>G</math> is called a ''<math>k</math>-rainbow coloring'' if for every set <math>S</math> of <math>k</math> vertices of <math>G</math>, there is a rainbow tree in <math>G</math> containing the vertices of <math>S</math>. The '''<math>k</math>-rainbow index''' <math>\text{rx}_k(G)</math> of <math>G</math> is the minimum number of colors needed in a <math>k</math>-rainbow coloring of <math>G</math>. A <math>k</math>-rainbow coloring using <math>\text{rx}_k(G)</math> colors is called a ''minimum <math>k</math>-rainbow coloring''. Thus <math>\text{rx}_2(G)</math> is the rainbow connection number of <math>G</math>.

Rainbow connection has also been studied in vertex-colored graphs. This concept was introduced by Krivelevich and [[Raphael Yuster|Yuster]].{{sfnp|Krivelevich|Yuster|2010}}
Here, the '''rainbow vertex-connection number''' of a graph <math>G</math>, denoted by <math>\text{rvc}(G)</math>, is the minimum number of colors needed to color <math>G</math> such that for each pair of vertices, there is a path connecting them whose internal vertices are assigned distinct colors.
